subtopic: MR. BENSON-CLARIFICATION OF STATEMENT IN DEBATE RESPECTING TRANSFER OF FUNDS
speechtext:
I should like to make a clarification of what I said yesterday as reported on page 9840 of Hansard, having to do with the Auditor General's request for funds to supplement his vote from finance vote No. 15 "Contingencies".
I find that the request referred to, which is contained in a letter from the Auditor General's office dated October 19, was for "an amount of $29,800 now requested for the month of November, 1966 to recoup our salary allotment". While no specific reference was made to the mid-November payroll, the request covered a number of salary items up to and including November 30.
Subsequently a check with the office of the Comptroller of the Treasury revealed that the full amount required was $53,000 and accordingly this amount was released by Treasury Board authority dated November 10 from finance vote No. 15, "Contingencies".

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again a request is made for reduction of quorum in a committee of the house.
This time I believe that there is a factor which adds some significance to the request of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on immigration, made up

of 36 members, 24 from the House of Commons and 12 from the other place. The quorum was set at 50 per cent of all the members of the committee which means that 18 or 19 members or senators had to be in attendance so that the committee may sit. Now, request is made to reduce the quorum to 12 members. The resolution adds also the following:
Provided that the two houses are represented. Since there are 12 senators on that committee, it would be enough for the 12 senators to be in attendance and one single member out of the 265 members of the House of Commons so that the committee may sit regularly and study any subject pertaining to immigration.
In my opinion, it would be a true indication of weakness and giving up of its rights on the part of the House of Commons, if we were to allow a committee to sit when only one representative of the House of Commons is in attendance and one of the results of that motion might be to let the Senate in the long run take over the said joint committee of the house and the Senate on immigration which could sit with only the 12 members from the Senate in attendance and only one representative of the House of Commons.
We can see in what predicament that committee would be placed. Then the House of Commons would leave its rights aside would give them up in favour of the other place and I find that situation quite abnormal. That committee is made up of 36 members and, in normal circumstances, the quorum would be 18 or 19, I think. This would mean that if the senators are in attendance, only six or seven members of the House of Commons must be present to have the quorum. I wonder why they want to reduce that quorum, since, and I am coming back again to that point because it is very important-there are several members in the House of Commons, such as my colleague, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), and myself, who do not sit on any committee, and who would be pleased to participate to the committee's business because we are interested in it; we are prepared to attend the sittings, to discharge our duty fully, and the hon. member of Sherbrooke will support me on that point. But we are not permitted to sit on the committees.
For instance, on the committee on finance, trade, and economic affairs, we are often obliged to wait or to start without quorum, even though members of parliament, such as the member for Compton-Frontenac, the member for Villeneuve and the member for
November 15, 1966



Red Deer (Messrs. Latulippe, Caouette and Thompson) are in attendance without being members of the committee. We are not members of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, but we attend all the sittings since we are interested in the business of the house. We take interest in the work we have been elected to perform. All those I named a moment ago are not even members of the committee but are taking part in the discussions, while those who are members do not attend and there is no quorum. That is completely illogical, Mr. Speaker.
Last week I made an appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Referring to his respect for minorities, I said he should have the same respect for our minority here, in this corner-three independent members-asking him to see that we are appointed to at least one committee. Personally, I expressed the desire to be appointed member of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. I have not missed one meeting of that committee; I have attended regularly. There are many Liberal and Conservative members who have not even attended one meeting of that committee; in fact, there are seldom more than nine or 10 out of 24 who attend. We are ready to attend the meetings; there are five or six members of the Ralliement Creditiste, Social Credit and our group, who consider it their duty to attend the meetings without being members. This should be taken into consideration and 'members who want to take part in the work of committees should be accepted as members.
I once again make a personal appeal to the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who are both responsible for the orderly pursuance of the business of this house and ask them to see to it that the members of the independent group are appointed to certain committees, since they are ready to work, to do their share and to cooperate. I think the Prime Minister should take the matter in hand personally and see to it that independent members, whose privileges are violated here, are appointed to committees.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) recalled the other day that he was on five committees. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I was not appointed to any committee.
Therefore, I repeat my request to the Prime Minister and I hope that he will remedy that situation which violates the most fundamental privileges of independent members.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister in connection with the repeated press references to the effect that Canada is leading other nations to bring about the setting up of a committee to enable the Secretary General of the United Nations to arrive at a plan whereby communist China may be admitted to the Security Council, and the Republic of China relegated to a position in the General Assembly. Is it a fact that these negotiations are going on, and that the United States and the empire of Japan are taking the strongest possible objection to Canada's action, which to both of them is retrogressive?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned in the house last week, Canada is engaged in consultations with other governments in preparation for the China item in the United Nations which will come up, it is understood, on November 18 in the General Assembly. The house will also recall that the Secretary of State for External Affairs told the General Assembly on September 26 of the growing opinion in Canada that if the United Nations is to realize its potential capacities we must make some further advance toward the objective of universality, particularly in regard to continental China which represents such a significant portion of the world's population. The Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out then, and I should like to stress again here, that there are fundamental obstacles lying in the way of resolving this issue, and it is not possible to predict whether this year's debate will be any more productive of a solution than have been those in the past.
Our consultations at the moment are concerned with the possibility of some further and equitable progress being made at this assembly toward universality of membership. It is too early to indicate whether or not it will be possible to do this.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister say whether or not Canada is joining with eight other nations to introduce a resolution in the United Nations, to which I have already previously referred in the house and, second, is it a fact that the strongest objection is being raised against communism by two of our major allies, the United States and Japan?
November 15, 1966

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the situation disclosed in the first part of the question addressed to me by the right hon. gentleman is not a fact in those terms, and therefore it follows that the second question does not require an answer.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary. In view of the statement made yesterday by Mr. Chester Ronning that China would not consider a two-Chinas policy, is the Canadian government investigating the policy of having the Formosa group known henceforth as Formosa rather than China, in an effort to make it possible for mainland China, the real China, to be brought into the United Nations?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting suggestion but is not one that is necessarily included in the ideas we are putting forward to our friends which in the normal course of events we would be doing, as this resolution will be coming up in the next few days. We have given much thought to the solution of this problem and one approach to it is by recognizing the "two-Chinas" policy.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA

Prime Minister whether before the vote takes place at the end of the debate on the resolution the government will make known to this house its definite stand on the general issue of the admission of continental China to the United Nations?

I would dearly love to see such quick action by this government to find the $25 million that on October 5, 1965, they promised would be available to the coal industry. How about some speed in fulfilling that promise? What is the government going to do about that situation? I do not criticize the fact that the minister of mines-I will refer to him as such although I understand the government has added natural resources to his responsibilities-did not go to Nova Scotia on November 3 and make clear the government's policy in this respect. I fully agree that his decision not to go was mutually agreed upon with a delegation that arrived in this city to talk to the government about the delay in carrying out the definite commitment it made on October 5, 1965. This promise has yet to be fulfilled. But prior to November 3-I do not recall the date; it was somewhere around the latter part of October of this year-the minister had already announced his intention to go to Sydney and explain the government's coal policy.
I repeat that his decision not to go was mutually agreed upon. But that week the government were examining the situation. I wish they would examine it with the same speed with which they examined a few other things very recently. Why must the miners and those concerned in the coal industry of Nova Scotia still wait for this assistance to be provided to the industry, when the minister of labour of that time referred to it as a definite commitment with no strings attached? I have already invited the Minister of Transport to come to my office and I will play the tape of the minister's statement in respect of this $25 million.
There has been no action in this regard. The delegation from the coal industry of Nova

Scotia met with several members of the cabinet, but there has yet to be any action taken in this respect. How long do we have to wait? Do we have to wait until another election is called so that the Liberals can put out a message at all the polling stations of Cape Breton South to the effect that the Liberal government deserves the vote of the people for what they have done for the Cape Breton miners?
This is what they did in November, 1965; the message was there for all the Liberal poll workers to use. I have said this before, but I say it again, that a poll worker of the Liberal party who made this message available to me said he was more interested in the welfare of the Cape Breton mines and miners than in the welfare of the Liberal party. He is prepared to give me an affidavit that this offer of $25 million to assist the industry was Liberal strategy, although the then minister of labour made this offer as a definite commitment on the part of the government.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, in 1965 the message to the voters of Cape Breton South was to the effect that the Liberal government deserved their vote this one time for what they had done for the Cape Breton miners and the coal industry. A Liberal will give me an affidavit to this effect. What have they done? What are they doing now? Are they perhaps waiting for another election to be called so they can come to my part of the country and say: We are a little late on our previous promise, but we will give you $30 million this time? Or will it turn out to be something like the 1919 promise with respect to medicare? Will we have to wait until the mines are completely phased out and the industry goes down the drain?
I am sorry that the minister involved is not in the chamber. In this connection, I will speak of the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The minister's remarks reveal a very patronizing attitude on his part. He is a very friendly and affable fellow. He said to the Cape Breton miners, in his own peculiar and very patronizing manner: You know, there isn't a man in Canada with more experience than me in closing mines. Then, he went on to tell the delegation that the minerals and ore bodies of this country are the responsibility of the provinces. Of course, he asked the question, what was provincial policy in this respect? He said, again in his patronizing way: We are not going to argue about who should take the initiative here.
I hope the government would not argue about who should take the initiative in attempting to solve this problem. There is no
November 15, 1966

argument left for the Grits. They look the initiative on October 5 when they went into Halifax and said they would make $25 million available to assist the Nova Scotia coal industry. There is no doubt that at the next cabinet meeting this question was discussed with the Prime Minister, who said the government would soon be coming forward with a decision. The other day an hon. member asked what he meant by "soon" and the answer was that it meant "in the very near future". But here we are, more than a year after that definite commitment was made by the government to assist the Nova Scotia coal industry, and nothing has been done. The same thing can be said of this government with regard to many, many other areas of the Canadian economy. They have taken no action whatsoever to solve these problems. No government has ever surpassed this government so far as audacity is concerned.
I understand that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been in the province making further references to the coal situation, but what he has said has apparently not been worth carrying in the press. Members on this side of the house have been pressing, with members of the New Democratic Party and others-and no doubt in the Liberal caucus pressure has been applied in this respect-for action to be taken to improve the situation of our old age pensioners. The other day the Prime Minister told this house emphatically that he was prepared to bring in old age pension legislation as soon as the opposition was ready. Well, Mr. Chairman, the opposition has indicated on many occasions that it is ready to deal with this legislation.
But how can we trust this government? There is no way in which any member on the government side of the house can convince me that there is any reason to believe what they say at any particular time on any particular subject. The emphasis again must be placed, of course, on the Minister of National Defence. When the accusation was made that the minister released classified information he denied it, although he failed to get to his feet to do so. speechtext: Order, may I inform the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.
Mr. Chairman, my sole purpose in taking part in the debate is to express the hope that we can bring a speedy end to this debate on interim supply.

May I ask the hon. member a question on this point? Is the hon. member aware that we are just waiting for the Minister of National Revenue to come back and answer a question which was asked on orders of the day and then, within a few minutes, we are prepared to bring this debate to a conclusion? The Minister of National Revenue is holding everything up.

If the Minister of National Revenue is going to make a statement and then the debate is to be concluded, I am quite prepared to forgo the privilege of taking part in the debate. However, I wish to say that I think interim supply presents the opposition parties with a very real opportunity to express views which they have not had the chance of presenting. We in the New Democratic Party, when the interim supply matter was raised, took the opportunity to present the whole matter of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines application to build a pipe line through the United States. We had no other opportunity to discuss that matter.
The Prime Minister had agreed from time to time that we would have an opportunity to discuss it but the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, without reference to parliament, tabled an agreement approving this application by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. We, therefore, felt that it was only right and proper that this matter should get a thorough airing. There is no doubt that as a result of that debate one thing has become abundantly clear, namely, that there is no national fuel policy in Canada. It is now perfectly clear that three years ago the National Energy Board recognized the need for twinning the lines in northern Ontario, that nothing was done by the government, and that the National Energy Board had no authority to do anything.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in speaking with some pride of the fact that this legislation was passed by the Conservative government, referred to the National Energy Board as being an office of records. Events

have proven that this is all it is, an office of records. It had no authority to compel the twinning of that line, with the result that we now have the situation where the government can claim that there will be a shortage of gas in southern Ontario. Since they can build the line through the United States faster, the government can claim this project should be proceeded with rather than the twinning of the northern line.
All of this demonstrates the lack of planning and the lack of any national fuel policy. We therefore feel that we were completely justified in raising this matter as we did. We have expressed our views on it, and we are certain that time will vindicate the position we have taken. As a matter of fact, if the Federal Power Commission in Washington does not approve this agreement, we will be back where we started. We will then have to twin the northern line after having wasted a considerable number of years in planning and discussing this project. However, having made our protest we are not going to hold up the estimates and we have not taken much part in the debate in recent days.
The other matter which has been raised in the house by the Conservative members is in regard to unification. Our view on it was expressed in one speech by the hon. member for Greenwood who pointed out that we need to have facts before we can intelligently cast a vote with respect to unification. We need to know what is the government's concept of Canada's military role in the present day world.
We should have the views of experienced military men who are both for and against the unification program. We need to know whether the proposed unification will give the Canadian people, to use an American expression, a better bang for a buck, and whether we will get a better defence system for the $1,600 million a year which we are spending on national defence. We, in this party, have supported the official opposition in their argument that there is a good deal of merit in sending the subject matter of the national defence bill to a committee so that both those who are for it and those who are against it may give testimony upon which we can make an intelligent judgment. I am sorry the government has not acceded to what I consider to be a very reasonable request.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
If the unification proposal has merit, surely it should be possible to defend it in committee. If it is defended effectively then, certainly, our party will give its approval to it. If it
November IS, 1966

cannot be proven effective, there will be amendments, and a better policy will result. Surely the government, does not want a Liberal, a Conservative or an N.D.P. defence policy. They want a Canadian defence policy. They want a policy that has the support of the majority of the members of the house and the support of most of the Canadian people. That can be obtained more easily by sending the subject matter of the bill to a committee of the House of Commons.
I notice that the Winnipeg Free Press, on Saturday, November 5, gave its wholehearted support to this idea. The Winnipeg Free Press is, as has been known for years, one of the chief apologists of the Liberal party. It is one of its chief proponents.
That is why that paper has been so busy.

These words appeared in the editorial:
While Mr. Hellyer on Friday agreed to turn the bill over to the Commons defence committee, where outside witnesses can be heard, he did so only on the condition that it first be given second reading. This, as Mr. Diefenbaker rightly pointed out, puts the Commons in the awkward position of having to vote approval of the bill in principle before it has had an opportunity to hear the views of those who opposed it. The minister is clearly attempting to ram the bill through as swiftly as possible, apparently in the hope of neutralizing in advance the testimony of expert witnesses. Legislation containing so many critical changes to the nation's defence structure should be given detailed study in committee before the House is asked to approve it in principle.
I think that states the position very well. I hoped that the government would have acceded to the request in the editorial, in order to bring the debate to an end. I know that the Minister of National Defence is anxious to prove that he is one of the strongmen in the cabinet. There are times when we confuse stubborness with strength. Sometimes stub-borness in a sign of weakness, a sign of basic insecurity.
While we want this unification bill to be sent to a committee of the house, we do not think that the government's stubborn refusal to do so warrants our continuing this debate any longer. We have made our plea with reference to the Trans-Canada pipe line, and the mismanagement of the project as well as the sellout. The Conservatives have made their protest, a prolonged protest, about the unification bill. There will be plenty of opportunity for discussion when the unification bill comes before the house again. It can then be discussed in further detail.

I wish to make a special appeal. Let us try to resolve this matter and end the debate. For one thing, we are using up days which ought to be devoted to other estimates. It is true that we can discuss some of these items in interim supply, but most of the ministers are absent, and there can be no consecutive discussion of departments. We are now rambling over a wide field. If we continue this interim supply debate for too long we shall use up time, as we are doing, which will be badly needed if we are to discuss some of the legislation which, in the opinion of this party, must be disposed of before Christmas. I have in mind particularly the legislation for old age pensioners which the government has not yet put on the order paper. The reason, I suspect, is that legislation is not ready. We ought at least to remove any semblance of an excuse that the government has for not putting it on the order paper, because this is vital legislation. It is vital to the welfare of many old people in this country, and we, in this party, want to see that legislation put on the order paper.
We want to see that legislation given top priority. We want it to be dealt with and passed. From the outline of it we have had there is much in it that is unsatisfactory, much that leaves a great deal to be desired. But, if it will ameliorate the conditions of the old people in this country, let us have it before the house and let us pass it.
The same is true with respect to the estimates providing increases of pensions for veterans, and I refer to disability pensions and veterans allowances. Also, there is the measure providing collective bargaining for civil servants, which is very pressing. Of course, the housing legislation ought to be passed at the earliest date because housing conditions in this country are appalling. While the housing legislation will do very little to improve the situation, at least we ought to do what we can. We ought to take what the government is prepared to give.
Medicare legislation ought to be passed, if at all possible, before Christmas. I am aware that the government intends to change the date, to make the legislation effective on July 1, 1968, but the fact remains that this is still important legislation and it ought to be put on the statute books as soon as possible. If the provincial governments are to pass concurrent legislation they need to know what the basic legislation will be. They need to know the terms and conditions which apply, in order that the provincial complementary legislation will be on all fours with that passed by the parliament of Canada. I hope, therefore, that

November 15, 1966
Interim Supply
we can finish this debate today, and that we can go as quickly as possible to some ol the other legislation I have mentioned.
I want to make a special appeal to the government. They have been stubborn about sending the unification bill to a committee. I hope they will not be equally stubborn about insisting that the unification bill should have top priority. I need not tell the government that if unification is dealt with before the other legislation I have mentioned is dealt with we will not get to the old age pension legislation, veterans matters, housing, medicare and collective bargaining for civil servants before Christmas. We could become involved in another flag debate-a protracted, interminable debate which would take a great deal of time and which would prevent parliament from dealing with some of the matters that are vital to many Canadians. After all, if unification does not come into effect until next spring, nobody will be hurt; nobody will be adversely affected. As a matter of fact, it might be advantageous to the government if it had some time to study this matter carefully. If the Minister of National Defence is right when he says that this legislation-and I quote him-"will establish Canada as the unquestionable leader in the field of military organization" then, surely, we ought to take time in making this dramatic step forward that according to the minister will put Canada in the vanguard of military institutions in the world.
Nobody will be hurt if unification has to wait until spring. But many people will be hurt if the old age pension legislation, medicare, veterans legislation, housing legislation and collective bargaining for civil servants are not dealt with between now and Christmas. I appeal to the government to deal with these matters before taking up the unification legislation. While this party will not wage a filibuster on unification, there is a distinct possibility that unification will project parliament into a stalemate, and the people I have mentioned who are dependent on the legislation I have enumerated will suffer in consequence.
Above all, I appeal to the house to consider what is being done to the prestige of parliament. I am sure that hon. members go to their constituencies from time to time, as I do. I need not tell them the prestige of parliament is at a low ebb. It is probably many years since the public has had such a low opinion of parliament and of the performance which we have been giving.

[DOT] (4:30 D.m.)
I think that for us to continue day by day to discuss unification or anything else when the people of Canada know that there are other items demanding our attention would be further to denigrate parliament in the eyes of the Canadian people.
I should therefore like to say that, as far as this party is concerned we urge that the present debate be ended as speedily as possible. We plead with the government that when this interim supply measure is passed some of the important items affecting the lives and the welfare of several millions of Canadians be given top priority, before we deal with unification. If the government will do this, I can assure them of our wholehearted co-operation in getting legislation on the statute books. I do not mean that we will forgo the right to express out opinions on these different pieces of legislation or to try to improve them where we think they need improvement. But there will be no frivolous opposition; there will be no obstruction. We want this leg:slation passed, not because it is government legislation but because it affords some modicum of hope and comfort for people in Canada who have been neglected too long.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I understood from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that the debate was to be closed after I had answered a question he had in mind. I would gladly yield the floor to the hon. member for Peace River.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre intended to indicate that he hoped this would be the case, but that I would have a contribution to make. It deals with the matter which the minister probably intends to mention, so with the indulgence of the committee. I would be prepared to make my contribution at this point.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It might be useful, then, if I gave my answer first, so that the hon. member might have this information which I am quite willing to give.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked for the mid-November payroll, which is estimated as follows: the total was $77,206,670 of which $17,031,450 was the payroll of the ten departments for which parliament had already granted full supply. This left a total of $60,175,220 to be met for the remaining departments. As already reported
November 15, 1966

to the house, the cash available in the votes was some $2,160,000 short of the figure required. I should like to assure members of the committee that there was no transfer from votes other than vote No. 15.
I have asked that a list be typed of all the votes concerned, the balance needed, the amount required for the mid-November payroll and the amount made up out of the $2,160,000, and with the permission of the house, as soon as this is typed, I propose to table these details which back up the figures I have now supplied.

I thank the minister for that information. Obviously, at this stage it would be d.fficult to formulate a rebuttal to the statement he has made. I assume that only in the due course of parliamentary audit, which I hope will be earlier rather than later, will it be really possible to examine within the four corners of each vote the details of how much money was paid, or needed, and how much was available. I say this without in any way controverting the minister's statements, which are the statements of the officials of his department.
Yesterday, I asked the Prime Minister a question in the following terms as reported at page 9840:
Regardless of the legal niceties or the merits, all of which can be argued later, in view of this further example of the erosion of parliamentary control over the executive does not the Prime Minister honestly feel that this whole matter of parliament vis-a-vis the executive should be the subject now of an earnest and anxious inquiry either by this house or a committee of the house?
We might relate that question to the facts which have formed the subject matter of the major part of the discussion which has taken place in this committee during the course of the present debate. First of these was the statement by the minister of defence that, in his opinion, the evidence given before committee by serving officers or civil servants must be subjected to a considerable degree of supervision by ministers and by the government. I must take it, from replies given by the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet, that this view is supported by the government.
Various constitutional arguments were advanced to show that this had been the practice in the past and would always be the practice in the future. This may be the case though I, for my part, would reject much of that argument. Moreover, Mr. Chairman, I would draw your attention to the fact that last year this house approved a government proposal
Interim Supply
which said, in effect: here is a new concept of parliamentary government and parliamentary control by the legislature over the executive; we intend for the first time to set up committees of the house and give them full power to examine in detail both the estimates, the spending proposals, and the legislative programs.
This statement by the government was, I suggest, a clear indication that we were to embark on a completely new era of legislative government. This committee system was to be something novel. I hoped the new system would turn out well. Many of us did. But I must say I have been bitterly disappointed by what we have seen thus far.
This question of the evidence has arisen. In the second place, we have witnessed the definite and repeated refusal of the minister and of the government to refer to the committee on defence the proposals contained in the unification bill. I made a suggestion to the Prime Minister which I thought was a reasonable one. It would have permitted the government to retain its contention that reference to the committee on the subject matter of the bill would have killed the bill. My suggestion was that the government should simply refer the first item of the estimates of the department to the committee, thus authorizing the committee to engage in the comprehensive and careful scrutiny which a novel concept of the kind contained in the proposed amendments to the National Defence Act should entail.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
There could have been an acceptance of that view with dignity, and without in any sense compromising the legal position which the government saw fit to adopt. But this was refused out of hand.
I point out to hon. members of the committee that in this day and age I agree, as I am sure do other hon. members, that we must invest any government with very substantial and very considerable powers. In this day and age of fast, rapid moving events, when a government is dealing with great industrial corporations, with great labour unions, in, matters which require rapid and immediate decision, I yield to the necessity of investing it with powers but on the condition that we retain in the House of Commons the opportunity to examine, to scrutinize, to check and to object. When that is taken away, then I think we are on the road to vesting this house with the character of a legislative body whose sole function will be to meet occasionally and

November 15, 1966
Interim Supply
say yes or no to government proposals. This, I suggest, is not what the vast body of experience over the generations has indicated should be the function of the House of Commons. That is the second point.
The third point was the measures adopted by the government in order to meet the civil service payroll. Now, for the purposes of my argument I am not going to enter into the merits of the debate which preceded that decision. It is and has been established, and is written into the foundations of parliamentary government, that we must retain at all times the right to refuse supply if, in our view, there is a legitimate and honest complaint which needs to be ventilated. As to whether or not it is an honest and legitimate complaint, in the final analysis not the government but the electorate will decide, and when a party takes that position it is entitled to maintain it.
What has the government done in this instance? Just a few minutes ago the minister indicated that he had taken a certain procedure with regard to the supply votes. Now with respect to that, as I say, I believe we will require a parliamentary committee and the Auditor General's report, which I hope will be produced quite shortly. But I want to turn my attention to vote 15, and to read to hon. members the wording of vote 15 which, I would point out, has changed over the years.
Vote 15, as it appears in the blue book of estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1967, reads as follows:
Contingencies-To supplement other votes and to provide for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen expenses not otherwise provided for including awards under the Public Servants Inventions Act-
When we turn back to the estimates for 1960, we find a completely different wording. At that time what is now vote 15 appeared as vote 116, and the wording was very different:
Miscellaneous minor or unforeseen expenses, subject to the approval of the Treasury Board, including authority to re-use any sums repaid to this appropriation-
Obviously there has been a change in the wording.
I would also point out, Mr. Chairman, that in 1960 the amount involved was slightly over $1 million. For the year 1967 the amount is $15 million in the original estimates, and we have no idea what it may yet come to when the supplementaries are added to it. As a matter of fact, for the preceding year the amount was $29 million.
I suggest that if you take these words in their proper legal sense, although I reserve

the right to argue that, it may well be that the government was justified in its course. But surely, it was never intended that a vote of this kind could be used by the government for the purposes to which the minister has put it.
I suggest this constitutes a violation of the the purposes to which the minister has put it.
I suggest this constitutes a violation of the principle of parliamentary control.
If the government can put $15 million in this vote, why can't it put $150 million in it? True enough, the matter comes back to the house. It is a vote; it is an appropriation, but a government with a majority has the right to do that, and no doubt certain governments will use that right. When I say governments, Mr. Chairman, I use the word "government" generally, although I must say the present government has a remarkable proclivity toward the undue exercise of executive power.
I suggest that such use of a vote of this kind constitutes a grave violation of the principle of parliamentary control, and I have with me some brief citations from some learned people who have considered this very same serious problem.
As a matter of fact, the history of this problem goes back to the year 1340 when the first recorded grant made to Edward III was for "the maintenance and safeguard of our said realm of England, and on wars in Scotland, France and Gascoign". There was a limit placed on the expenditure. Since that time that principle has been maintained, but today it is being whittled away, step by step, stage by stage.
Responsible government cannot be a reality if the control of expenditure is surrendered to the treasury, and this is a surrender to the treasury. The right of parliament to control taxation and appropriation is based on common law, but of course it is now given statutory form. Most contemporary writers on the subject agree that parliamentary control of finance is in danger of becoming non-existant, and that it is high time parliament did something about it.
The decline of parliamentary influence is one of the effects of this development, and the problem of restoring parliamentary effectiveness is a matter of improving the means of informing parliament, a means which I hoped would have been found within the limits of the committee system which the government set up but which, in my humble opinion, has now proved to be almost useless.
I submit that here, in this one instance, the refusal to allow serving officers to give their
November 15, 1966



own untrammelled, unhampered and undoctored evidence; the refusal to reconvene the defence committee to consider the principle that is involved in the defence bill; and finally, what the government has now done within the brief space of the few weeks we have considered this matter, constitute three flagrant violations of the responsibility of the executive to the legislative branch of government. I feel, Mr. Chairman, I could not allow this debate to conclude without setting on the record my views and the alarm I feel at the trend 1 see developing.

November 15, 1966
Interim, Supply
somehow the United States will not be able to develop its industry and that we will gain thereby an advantage over it. I think Mr. White spelled this out very clearly in his remarks when he said that the development ot new markets in the United States would be met by increased exploration and development within that country. His great fear seemed to be that the arrangement with Canada would be completed before the American competition became a factor.
1 was pleased to hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam express concern about medicare and urge that it be put through very quickly. The reason he gave was that if the provinces are to be in a position to pass enabling legislation, then they must know the details of the bill. I hope this is an indication that his party is going to be in favour of a variety of amendments which need to be made to that legislation before it is enacted and becomes the law of the country. Perhaps we can be hopeful there. I felt that this was welcome news.
We in the Social Credit party are concerned about the priorities in respect of the legislation which is before the house. We have not taken part in this debate on interim supply, with the exception of a brief speech by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and a few remarks by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. We feel the defence issue can be handled through the regular processes of the house. We were happy to hear that the Minister of National Revenue found some money the other day. We always are happy to hear that the Minister of National Revenue can find money. We hope he might be able to find a little more for things like national housing and perhaps the HARP project. Admittedly, he did not find it through some of the sources we might have suggested to him, but none the less he found it.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-241, to amend the National Housing Act, 1954.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when winding up the discussion on this bill during the resolution stage I expressed my deep appreciation to all hon. members who had participated in the debate, and particularly to those who had made constructive suggestions which warranted earnest consideration. In this connection, I should like to refer particularly to the well-reasoned comments on this complex and important subject put forward by the hon. members for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and others.
I also said on Thursday, October 27, to deal later with certain matters raised during the course of the earlier debate. The various views put forward point out the multitude of factors involved in the spectrum of housing. They also reflected the abiding concern of members from all corners of this house in the development of national housing legislation which will benefit all Canadians regardless of their station in life.
It is understandable, therefore, that some members who participated in the debate at the resolution stage voiced the opinion that even more aggressive steps should be taken at this time to bolster housing generally in Canada. Certainly, it had been the government's wish-perhaps I should say the government's intention-to bring forward more changes to the National Housing Act at this session. These changes would give important new significance to this legislation in preparation for future housing regulations in this rapidly expanding nation.
November 15, 1966

Indeed, as I mentioned during the resolution stage, discussions I had had on behalf of the government with most of the provinces during the past year, did go beyond the measures that we are now proposing in this bill. It is our opinion, however, that in the present economic climate such proposals as can reasonably be deferred in respect of housing should be deferred at this time. As a consequence, the bill before us represents only those improvements that are deemed absolutely essential at the present time.
Through a moderate extension to the present loan provisions of the National Housing Act, Bill C-241 provides assistance for the purchase of existing housing. I think all hon. members will agree that this is a timely step, particularly in meeting the home-ownership needs of lower and middle income families in Canada. Initially the regulations governing such assistance-that is assistance which will be provided if this bill becomes law-will limit the amount of a loan by establishing a ceiling.
The provisions will at the same time require that repairs and improvements be of a minimum value. In other words, we are not going to make national home loans for the purpose of assisting people in buying existing housing for resale. This involves a combination approach and will involve a purchase and require a minimum improvement of perhaps $1,000, or something slightly higher. It is difficult to conceive of anything less than $1,000 in this regard or anything much more than perhaps $2,000 or $3,000. However, if an individual wanted to use eight tenths of the loan for repairs, as long as he complied with the regulations, that would be possible. I might say in respect of the amount of repairs, whether they be valued at $1,000 or a larger amount, they can be met wholly or in part by work by the prospective homeowner. In other words, if he is a good carpenter, brick layer or electrician, the work that he and the members of his family can do will be included as part of his contribution toward the cost of the house.
I am sure that hon. members can appreciate the significance of this new type of loan to the thousands of potential homeowners in Canada, particularly those in the lower and middle income brackets. Many people today cannot afford new housing, but they do want to own their own homes. As has been previously pointed out, you can buy an existing home, some several decades old, which would be very comfortable for perhaps another several decades with the addition of a modern heating
National Housing Act system, a modern lighting system or a modern plumbing system. Up to this time, many families in these income brackets have not been able to purchase homes of their own, that is of the kind that meet with various building by-laws in different towns or cities, for less than $14,000 to $15,000, and in some cases even higher. People in the lower and middle income brackets cannot afford to own that type of house. They may be able to rent them but they cannot afford to buy them. As a result of this amendment, which will offer the benefits of low interest and long-term loans, people who wish to purchase these dwellings will receive exactly the same terms they would receive if they were purchasing new houses.
Some hon. members have asked me more than once whether or not an increase is contemplated in the $4,000 maximum allowable under the home improvement provisions of the act. As hon. members know, under the National Housing Act, a person who owns a house and wants to improve it can go to his bank or to a lending institution and borrow up to $4,000 at a reasonable interest rate, and repayment of the loan will be guaranteed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is a fact that this takes care of the owners of existing homes. The proposed amendment to which I have referred will take care of those people who want to buy existing houses and a person who wishes to continue living in his own house, who can borrow up to $4,000 in order to make repairs to such house is also provided for. In giving consideration to whether the $4,000 limit should be increased, we made a careful study of the situation and we found that the average loan over a period of several years, including the last two or three years when a substantial number of loans were made, has been about $1,500. So we consider that, for the present at least, the $4,000 level is adequate at the present time; but this level can be changed if the circumstances so dictate.
I must say-I think this is an appropriate time to deal with this matter-that I listened with great surprise to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) during the resolution stage. My interest deepened with his statistical presentation reviewing this year's housing performance against the housing performance of 1965. We all know that statistics are open to many interpretations, depending upon who is doing the explaining or the interpreting, and who is quoting the statistics. But I must say

November 15, 1966
National Housing Act
that the hon. member's comparison of a full year's activity in 1965 with only seven months activity in the current year is hardly a fair comparison and is certainly not the kind of picture that one would expect to have presented by a member of this house.
I believe that if the hon. member will look at the statistical table with which I provided him on October 5, he will be able to readily verify that the current housing situation is not nearly as dire or disappointing as he has suggested. The hon. member also expressed the opinion that the present amendments will be no more significant in solving Canada's housing problems than the changes enacted by this house in 1964. I can only express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that the new proposals contained in this bill will be equally as effective as those passed by parliament in 1964. Hon. members will recall the principal changes to the act two years ago. They involved widened assistance for urban renewal, and the introduction of high-ratio loans, as an alternative to the usual federal-provincial partnership arrangements for public housing. I have no hesitation in stating that the growing wave of urban renewal activity that we now have in Canada is due largely to the amendments that were passed in 1964.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, since those amendments became law in the early summer of 1964 almost every major city in Canada has entered this field or has increased its activity and its interest in this area. Today almost every major city in the country, and many smaller municipalities, have under way or in the planning stages, largely financed by reason of those 1964 amendments, programs to eliminate blight and slum conditions from their communities. This was one of the outstanding achievements made at that time in the field of housing-because that program is closely associated with housing. I should like to stress that we art still only in the initial stages of this developing national venture to improve our total living environment. However, I think it is significant to note that in the first nine months of 1966 almost $16 million have been committed from the federal treasury for urban renewal activities, as against only slightly more than $4 million in the full year 1965.
Included in this year's total for the nine-month period are grants for 25 urban renewal studies, as against 21 similar grants in 1965. Contributions have also been extended in 1966 for the development of proposals for 16 urban renewal schemes, while $15.3 million have been authorized for the actual implementation of major civic improvement programs in Toronto, Calgary, Burnaby, British Columbia,

Windsor, Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and other cities.
Coming back to the question of housing for people of low income, I should like to point out that in the province of Ontario N.H.A. loan assistance for public housing has been adapted and activities in this field have been accelerated greatly in the past four years. Between January and the end of September of this year, more than 40 developments have been undertaken by the Ontario Housing Corporation in municipalities in all parts of the province, with 90 per cent of the many millions of dollars involved being provided by the federal government through the National Housing Act. It is true that this money is advanced by way of loan, but, without these large loans to the Ontario Housing Corporation, this tremendous development in the provision of thousands of houses every year to those people in the province who must live in public housing would not have been possible.
Several questions were asked last month concerning our intentions in regard to loans for student housing, which is dealt with in this bill. Here, I may simply say that it is our opinion that financial aid for the housing of students should be extended wherever the need exists, always provided that the province concerned joins in the request that the funds be made available. There must be the concurrence of the province, because they have the prime responsibility in the field of education.
Before I resume my seat, I might refer briefly to the statistics quoted by several hon. members concerning Canada's housing needs over the next four years. In determining the figure applicable to the current year I believe that the hon. members to whom I have referred rather simplified the calculation by assuming that housing requirements would be equal each year for the next four years. This is certainly not borne out by the report that was quoted by hon. members in this connection. The report forecast an accelerating rate of housebuilding which was to reach its peak in 1970; so to pick out 1966 is not representative of the peak that will not be reached until four years from now.
It is with the knowledge of this growing demand for housing that we are asking in this bill for very substantial increases in the amount of funds that will be available for direct lending. This year, for instance, we are committed and have practically made arrangements to provide direct loans for 31,500 houses at an average cost, I believe, of $15,000 or $16,000 per unit. Therefore, we need money
November 15, 1966

to continue our direct lending in the years ahead. We also need money to take care of the insured, the approved lenders.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
They also are provided for in the bill.
Another aspect of N.H.A. activity provided for in the bill, and referred to in earlier debates, concerns aid for housing in the small communities and rural areas. I certainly appreciate the concern of hon. members who represent rural areas, in fact the concern of all members of this house, and I can only say that the policies governing direct loans by C.M.H.C.-and that is all we can deal with today because the private lenders must take care of other fields-reflect the concern about obtaining mortgage assistance for anyone who wants to make a direct loan from C.M.H.C. whether he lives in a city or a town. It is true that it is more difficult for such a person to approach C.M.H.C. if there is no office conveniently located to where he resides. This is one reason I hope for much more help in the field of housing when the amendments to the Bank Act, which are now before the committee, have been passed. If parliament approves the legislation, our banks will be able to make loans on the same terms as those provided by C.M.H.C. or by the traditional lending institutions.
As regards the smaller communities, the new amendments which permit the purchase and improvement of existing houses should have a tremendous effect for all of them. This is particularly important during the winter months when work can be done on partially completed houses. Improvements can be made on houses during the winter months as well as in the summer. I hope that the additional funds which will be made available for the purchase and improvement of existing houses, will be put to use this winter because people do not wish to move from the smaller communities in which they live and there is some seasonal unemployment in many parts of Canada. Tradesmen with skills in the housing and construction industries can work on improving the existing houses regardless of whether they are plumbers, electricians or other tradesmen.
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill will encourage the building and improvement of low rental housing, and here the loan ratio is important to the smaller communities.
I do not think it is necessary to emphasize that the amendments which we are introducing at this time are all measures which the government believes contain an element of
National Housing Act
urgency, not only in meeting housing needs but in helping winter employment. I therefore urge all hon. members to support the early passage of this bill because every day counts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOAN RATIO ON RENTAL HOUSING, LOANS ON EXISTING HOUSING, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic Party are deeply disappointed with the amendments to the National Housing Act set forth by the minister. We would prefer a complete overhaul of the act dealing with some of the more fundamental problems with which we are faced in housing today. At present we are experiencing the worst shortage in housing that has ever prevailed in Canada. During the debate at the resolution stage of the bill, the minister indicated that this year housing in Canada has declined by 23 per cent over last year, and this in itself is very serious. He had hoped that the decrease would have stayed at 10 to 15 per cent, but figures have thus far shown that the decrease is proceeding at the rate of 23 per cent.
I wish now to refer to an article in the Globe and Mail of November 4 dealing with the housing shortage. It reads as follows:
Housing starts in urban areas dropped to 8,427 in August from 15.522 a year previously, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. In the first eight months of 1966, starts declined to 65,578 from 87,185.
Last year the housing starts in Canada amounted to approximately 166,000. This year we will be very fortunate if we reach 130,000 housing starts. Again this indicates the serious decline in housing which we are now experiencing in Canada. One may ask what is the reason for the serious decline? The quick answer would be that it is the high cost of mortgages. The minister, in his statement on the resolution, indicated quite clearly that the sources of the conventional lenders for the financing of housing in Canada had dried up, beginning in the month of February. This only left the C.M.H.C. to provide the money for new homes, with the obvious result that the gap has not been filled.

I wonder whether banks will be willing to make loans at rates lower than those offered by conventional lenders. At the present time, conventional lenders provide loans for a first mortgage at 7.5 to 8 per cent, which has discouraged many people from buying homes.

The important legislation applies to many senior citizens across Canada who have homes they would like to repair but, because of limited income, are unable to do so. The government could overcome this situation by bringing in an amendment giving senior citizens loans at 3 per cent to make necessary home repairs. It is frightful that a person in the twilight of life who has bought a home, who is now faced with high municipal taxes, should be faced with problems in connection with home improvements which are created by high interest rates. The way to overcome such problems is by making home improvement loans available to these people at a low interest rate.
I turn to the problem of urban renewal. The minister waxed eloquent on urban renewal. He must be given full credit for the improvement which has taken place in this area. May I point out some of the difficulties which have been experienced with urban renewal. I hope the minister deals with these through amendments. The difficulty facing people in urban areas has to do with relocation. People are asked to give up their homes, homes which are often adequate and sufficient for their needs. They are asked to give them up for urban renewal, and they have to find other homes. Often, there are not other adequate homes in their area, so that you find retired people who have paid for their homes being forced to move into apartments until the urban renewal people have taken care of them and brought them back into an apartment or other accommodation in their own area. Sometimes those people have to buy a home costing 25 per cent more than a similar home in the area from which they were asked to move.
With the high interest rates, what I have just mentioned forms one of the main difficulties in urban renewal. Another difficulty-and in this the minister can play a vital role-has to do with compensation for people asked to move. The minister can say that expropriation is a provincial matter, and that he is bound by expropriation acts. It is up to the minister, the provincial ministers and the municipal officials, to bring about changes in the expropriation acts, so that people who are asked to move because of urban renewal are compensated for the forcible taking. This would enable them to buy a home in an area similar to the one from which they have moved. Often, people affected by urban renewal have to buy homes costing 20 to 30 per cent more than
National Housing Act
their own accommodation. The restrictive interpretation of the law which says that compensation is to be for the value of the home at the time of taking works a hardship on the people affected.
I hope that the minister, in dealing with the urban renewal scheme, will make sure that people affected are properly relocated; that they are properly compensated for the forcible taking, and for any difference they must pay in purchasing a new home. Also, some consideration ought to be given to any mortgage that may have to be assumed on the new home.
Some people say that if they are asked to move the least the government should do is offer interest free loans with which to buy other houses. The minister might say that this does not come within the ambit of the National Housing Act, but it illustrates the necessity for a department of housing and urban affairs.
In the short time I have been here I have developed a great deal of respect for the minister. I can appreciate that he has problems in fields other than housing. Difficulties connected with labour have taken up most of his time in the past, and he has neglected housing.
[DOT] (5:40 D.m.)
We have now reached the stage at which housing has become of such importance that a new ministry should be set up to deal with housing and urban affairs, one which could bring together ministers from the different levels of government to work out solutions to the difficulties we face in the field of urban renewal.

The present restrictions limiting loans to universities only have caused hardship to other, equally deserving institutions. The minister has been told about the experience of the vast polytechnic institute in Toronto, the great expansion which has taken place there and of the corresponding need to provide accommodation for students, most of whom come from outside Toronto. I trust that the minister's definition of the institutions now eligible for assistance is wide enough to cover private institutions.
I believe I have now dealt with the main amendments which the minister is bringing forward. Once again, I express the hope that a separate ministry will be set up to deal with the serious housing shortage and make sure

National Housing Act
that we have a housing policy adequate to meet the needs of all Canadians. For several years now, there has been quite a housing shortage in that vast area and it seems that the authorities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have been loath to facilitate the granting of loans in that area.
Many applications have reached us from the city of Amos, and we have just learned that the corporation can no longer grant loans.
There are people at present who have to live in houses located eight, ten or twelve miles from the city. The husband must travel morning and night to and from his work. He wishes to occupy with his family, as soon as possible, a house in the city. But the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation refuses loans, on the pretext that it does not have the necessary funds to meet the present demand.
I would like to ask the minister whether the increase of funds he asks for in this bill will enable the corporation to meet the demand coming from our cities, Amos, La-Sarre, Val d'Or, Malartic and Rouyn. I mention these because they are the most important in our area. I ask him whether this amendment to the act will enable the corporation to grant as early as this fall the loans

required. I point out also to the minister that we have, especially in Amos, many young students who attend educational establishments in Amos. They come from outside and they need a place to live. It is customary in that city for young people to rent a room in a private house; this helps the owner to pay for his house, to meet his commitments without burdening his budget and even sometimes shorten the repayment period, thus reducing interest which is sometimes quite considerable.
I therefore urge the minister to use his influence in order that the loans requested by that community may be granted as soon as possible and the building of these houses started as early as this fall, which will meet the present requirement.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I would like to make another remark to the minister concerning the models or plans of houses offered to those who want to build a house. I have noticed many times that most plans, which are prepared in advance, provide for one or two bedrooms-seldom three -and most plans offered are for houses much too small to meet the needs of families and accommodate our large families.
I therefore urge the minister to encourage architects, through competitions of all kinds, to present to the public a greater variety of housing plans likely to meet all the requirements and all the needs of our population.
I revert to my own region, the constituency of Chapleau, to point out to the minister that there is much room for improvement in the inspection of houses built under loans from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or from insurance companies or other approved lending companies. In fact, there is but one inspector to cover this whole vast area, and he lives in Val d'Or. Then, when his services are required to inspect the construction work of a house, we have to wait several days, indeed sometimes a few weeks, before he visits the site. This often involves complications and considerable delays.
Now, I would like to call the minister's attention to a particular case, to illustrate fully what I am now asking of him.
During the 1964-65 season, in the town of Amos-I am now referring to the winter housebuilding incentive program and to the $500 bonus-a house was started in the fall, and the inspection thereof was carried out only on February 2, 1966. Therefore, as can be expected in several cases of this type, the builder lost his patience and went ahead
November IS, 1966

with the construction without waiting for the preliminary inspection which should have been done before November 15, 1965. Now, when the inspector showed up on February 2, he found that the construction had exceeded the stage of the installation of the ground floor joists and refused payment of the $500 bonus, because the house in question did not meet the requirements of the act at the time of inspection.
I will point out to the minister that from November 15 to February 2, is indeed quite a long period and, if we had had an adequate organization in our area, the inspection could have been done at the appropriate time and that individual could have obtained justice, because it has been proven that as of November 15, his construction was not advanced further than required by the act.
Therefore, I wish to bring to the minister's attention that injustice against Mr. Briere, of Amos, who was denied the bonus he had requested and to which he was entitled, since the inspection was not carried out on the specified date, for lack of time on the inspector's part.
The inspector is not the only one to blame, for he must cover a large territory and it is obvious that his burden is too heavy. I therefore point out this fact to the hon. minister, so that the whole file in question may be reconsidered and the $500 bonus granted. It has been admitted this amount was not sufficient, but nevertheless quite appreciable when it comes to building a home. If this individual built his house during winter, it was for the purpose of moving into it and, at the same time, taking advantage of this bonus.
Those are the comments that I wanted to submit to the hon. minister upon consideration of Bill C-241 and I would like the minister to give it very special attention and study them carefully, so that the needs of the people in many constituency may be met and so that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may better serve our area, by opening a second office, if necessary, or increasing the number of inspectors in that office at the present time.

National Housing Act
It is passing strange to me that this house can be so indignant and vocal over suggested changes in our defence structure, and then appear so indifferent to legislation designed to assist in the development and maintenance of the institutions which form the very basis and bulwark of the nation we want to defend, namely, our homes. Mr. Speaker, if I remember correctly, at six o'clock I was referring to the fact that in so far as the provision of housing is concerned we are operating at this time almost to full productive capacity. There is a shortage of skilled labour which has tended to push up construction costs. Tight money has been instituted on a number of occasions in an attempt to correct this problem.
If there is a serious shortage of skilled labour which is hampering activities in the house construction field, this is an indictment of the government's policies on immigration and the retraining of our own citizens. The government should have anticipated this situation and made appropriate provisions. In this way we could have avoided interference with the forward movement and development of our economy in relation to the cost of houses in Canada. The average cost of a house in Canada is prohibitive so far as the lower income earners are concerned.
At this time I should like to refer to a memorandum presented by the Canadian Labour Congress to the government of
November 15, 1966

Canada. It is dated February 15 and at page 26 the following is stated:
The National Housing Act has yet to be of significant value to those with low incomes. The provisions of the act and the activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have succeeded in providing housing for those who, generally speaking, already had sufficient income to obtain it or who needed only some help in doing so. Those with very low incomes, and by this we mean wage earners with low earnings, the elderly on small pensions or social assistance and other needy elements in the community, continue to live in congested quarters, in substandard housing and in blighted areas or slums. They are the unwilling heirs of the cast-off housing left behind by the more fortunate members of the population. To make matters worse, they are often compelled to pay unduly high rents for the unsatisfactory facilities that are available to them.
I am sure that the minister and members of this house are aware of the problem in relation to the constantly increasing cost of homes. It is really a serious problem for which a solution must be found which will enable individuals in these income brackets to own their own homes and thereby establish a certain measure of security.
Interest rates constitute a real deterrent to home ownership. Let me refer to another paragraph in the memorandum to which I referred. At page 27 we find the following:
At the same time, we are aware, as you must be, that more Canadians could own their own homes if the burden of mortgage interest were lower. The rates established by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take this into account to some extent but insufficiently so. We believe that lower interest rates would be in order and urge you to give this early consideration. We feel also that a larger degree of mortgage indebtedness should be permissible on the purchase of older homes.
We realize that there is continual pressure on available capital for the provision of housing, which has caused a great difficulty in the mortgage field. We in the Social Credit party have for many years advocated a means whereby this pressure could be eased. The government should get out of the borrowing field and let the Bank of Canada take over. This would release a sufficient amount of capital in other areas and sectors of our economy so that private enterprise could provide a sufficient amount of mortgage money. The government should look into the whole matter very carefully because this is a sound and practical means of alleviating the situation. We in this party urge that consideration be given to using the Bank of Canada to finance projects in the social field and thereby leave other available capital for private investment and development.
National Housing Act
We in this party have read the provisions of the bill and agree with them as far as they go, but we urge the government to do more. That is all I have to say at the moment, but when we are considering the various clauses perhaps we will be able to make a further contribution.
